title: Moments of Realization
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett tells two stories of acceptance from a single morning and then turns to the breathing chapter of Shunryu Suzuki's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind. The first story is a late board report for Mindfulness Northwest, where picturing each board member's face while addressing an email softens the agitation, and the sun breaks through the clouds. The second is NPR's report on the 2020 fire that killed at least 9,000 mature giant sequoias, which brings up Nomon's own part in the climate crisis, along with heat pumps. Suzuki's image of the throat as a swinging door leads Nomon to feel the diaphragm moving like a jellyfish, and to recall a two-hour sit in a Bellingham park pavilion.

sentences.text: Got it, Zoom Lady.
Okay.
There's a little opening chant.
Please chant along if you know it, or do whatever you want to do.
*An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's words.*
Good morning again, everybody.
It's nice to have this gathering, and it feels more, interesting how something feels more precious if we don't have it for a while.
I guess we're just wired that way.
Thanks as always to Chris for coordinating these.
Great part of her role, she does so much for Red Cedar as our tanto, head of practice.
Thank you to Kate for jumping in, I think a little bit last minute, on all the bells and timing, and Talus for being our technical puppet master.
And I want to thank everyone here for being here.
I'm sure there are lots of other people who would love to be here, but something else is going on, as it goes.
I also wanted to mention my gratitude, and I don't know what the feeling is exactly, but we're starting, as you might know, a capital campaign, a big fundraiser.
We'll see if we can raise the funds needed to have a building in Bellingham to access regularly and maybe even own, if one can own anything, exactly like that, the way we think we can.
Although someone was just telling me yesterday, I've gotten to do sangha events three days in a row here, even though we don't.
I feel like making air quotes around everything, right?
Because it's all concepts, you know.
We don't have a building, but somehow we do a lot of stuff, and somebody was just telling me, "Wow, Red Cedar is so active.
There are so many options," you know.
So many things we can do together and ways we can practice together, so it'll work out in one way or the other for sure.
It's already working out.
It's always working out.
But deep bow, thank you to everybody who's thinking about this and has made a pledge, or has even started to turn a pledge into a donation, or is thinking about making a pledge.
We have a wonderful consultant who has a lot of experience with these things, and his advice is to really feel into our confidence and our excitement.
So I'm doing that, but our way is also to be open and transparent.
So I think I'm also a little bit nervous and freaked out about the whole thing.
The goal is impressive.
You can see all about that on the website, or check your mailbox.
We'll send you something if we have your mailing address.
So it's interesting to try to accept the way things are, isn't it?
It's such a core idea in practice, this idea of acceptance.
And we have so much material to work with always, whether it's a first-in-our-lifetime pandemic or another first-in-our-lifetime something, because it's always a first-in-our-lifetime something.
I noticed this morning two examples, I guess, of working with acceptance in my little sphere of reality.
A big example and a smaller example.
I feel like I need air quotes.
Big, small, what does that mean?
Anyway, here's the nominally small example.

Another event I have this afternoon, also on Zoom, is a board meeting for my other major role, the other organization that I also founded and direct, a mindfulness training organization called Mindfulness Northwest.
And a little sidebar: one of the sangha events I got to do recently, it occurred to me after ten years that maybe it'd be nice to offer that style of practice to Red Cedar.
So we did a little day of mindfulness in that style on Friday.
It was nice.
I really appreciate those of you who could come, and it seemed to be really well received.
So I'll do it again sometime if you couldn't make that one.
So anyway, for that organization, I have a board meeting this afternoon.
As the director, it's pretty much on me to provide the board members with some information, like an agenda and a board report.
I got some help from our treasurer with the financials, but it was my job to put it all together into a nice little package.
And I didn't get to it.
I've been really busy, even busier than usual, which is saying a lot for me.
So this morning I was feeling stressed about that.
I meant to do that yesterday.
Oh, I meant to do it yesterday.
You're supposed to have that out to your board members at least three days in advance, wouldn't you say?
It's an unwritten rule.
But the situation is a little different from the Red Cedar Zen board.
In the Red Cedar Zen community, the board is quite involved operationally, and it's a whole different thing.
This board is more of an oversight board.
If you have any nonprofit, you need a board of directors, and as the director and founder, I don't own it.
I just work there.
I work for the board.
But still, I felt bad.
I felt a little agitated.
I wasn't totally aware when this was percolating in me that I felt that way.
But what happened was, as I was rushing through the dishes, feeling squeezed for time and thinking, "Oh, I've got to finish preparing the talk and I've got to squeeze in this board report."
Squeeze in.
What does that even mean?
Do we think somehow we can create more time with that idea that we could squeeze in something?
Although I definitely do see that time doesn't run exactly in the linear way, I think it does.
It doesn't seem to run that way either.
I don't know if there is any squeezing in.
So I sat down at my computer to do these two things squeezily and simultaneously.
But the talk being first in the day, I knew I had to get that done first, right?
And an idea popped into my head as I was in this agitation.
Well, I thought to myself, I could at least send the board members a little note and say, "I'm looking forward to seeing you.
Here's the Zoom link.
And don't worry, I'm working on the report and the agenda.
It'll be here soon.
It'll be here soon."
As if they were sitting around with nothing to do today, each of them waiting for this document, as if they'd even noticed its absence, right?
But that's how I felt.
That's how one feels: we feel obligated and we're screwing up and we're behind and we're not doing quite right.
It's very stressful.
But as I filled in each of their email addresses to send this little email, coming soon, I noticed a little image of each of them popped into my mind.
And I know some warmth and appreciation arose in my heart and my body.
I felt that it was like a two-way relational thing, even though they weren't present in front of me at that moment.
I was feeling my appreciation for each of them for taking this volunteer role and supporting me and that organization.
And I was able to remember that they do it because they appreciate me and the organization.
They're not standing in judgment over how quickly I get them stuff.
And in fact, they probably won't even have time to look at it if I'd sent it three days ago anyway.
But not that rationalization is important here so much as the warmth and the feeling of connection.
And in that moment, it all shifted.
I could really feel my energy shift, my belly relax, my eyes and my cheeks soften.
And oddly, I was sitting by the window on our usual Bellingham gray morning, and the sun broke through the clouds at that very moment.
So I literally saw the light and relaxed.
It's so interesting about little moments of realization like this.
They're very ordinary, but they're also very important, right?
Very transformational.
And the curious thing about realization is that the moment before you have that realization, you don't yet have it.
The moment before, I was tense, a little upset, agitated, not even fully aware of all that was happening, a lot of tension in the body.
And then it came into view that it was okay, and there was this great release.

And then there was also some space for some curiosity about the story behind that story, how this seems to tie in to some deep underlying fears, fears of being ultimately inadequate in some way, not good enough, a fraud.
I didn't go to executive director school, I'm just making this up, you know?
Somehow it seems like anxiety always loops back to something deeper, and then it's okay at that surface level of worrying about the task.
But maybe there's also a little bit of healing in this deeper frame.
From the wonderful Yogachara Buddhist model, maybe a wholesome seed is planted, the seed of "it's okay, just as it is.
It's not a problem."
But the key point here isn't that I had a lot of great ideas that I could tell you about, although that's handy when you want to give a talk.
It's more about an experience.
We all have these kinds of experiences, I think.
But they're fleeting, and we forget about them and rush on to the next thing.
But maybe these moments are actually pretty important to our lives and to each other, to all society and the whole planet.

Be more aware of these dynamics, these tensions, these fears, these moments of acceptance and shift, these moments of peace, these moments of remembering at some level, maybe a deep level, if there's deep and shallow exactly in all this, that we're okay.
And it's okay.
And although there's a lot to do and some very deep and important problems to address, we can't address them in that way.
It's not going to work.
Maybe as we release into a little more acceptance and peace, it becomes more possible to show up and help.
At least I assume so.
We'll see when four o'clock rolls around if the board members are as kind and gracious as I think they'll be.
Maybe one of them will say, "Can we get another agenda item?
I would like to have more timely reporting."
Thank you very much.
We'll see.
But here's a little harder example.
And I'm sure your mind is thinking of many hard examples, because our minds are so good at that.
As I was rushing to get through the dishes so I could squeeze in the thing that I wasn't going to be able to squeeze in, I put NPR on the stereo in the kitchen.
And there was a feature on something that I had read about a few weeks ago.
I think I didn't really let it in.
It's about trees.
Like many of us here, I really love trees.
And some of the most amazing trees I've ever met are the giant sequoias that live in the Sierra Nevada mountains of California.
Have you ever seen them?
They're massive for one thing, and we're always impressed by big, right?
Up to 40 or so feet in diameter, more than 200 feet tall.
And they can live so long, at least 2,000 years and probably closer to 3,000.
At that point, the dendrochronology gets a little fuzzy.
You know, even in a 40-foot-wide tree, fit 3,000 rings in there and they've got to be pretty hard to tell.
But they're absolutely, I'm pretty sure, the largest trees in the world, and nearly the longest lived.
Oddly, California also has another species that's even older, which is probably the oldest tree, the bristlecone pine.
Not that far either, on the eastern slopes of the same mountains, they can live like 5,000 years.
You can believe that.
And they're not so big.
They're small and gnarled and gritty looking.
That's another story.
Back to giant sequoias.
There's not that many of them left.
They did better in a previous wetter, warmer era, or in a wetter and cooler era, sorry.
But now they live on in discrete groves scattered around the Sierras.
You don't find them everywhere.
But live on they do, for so long.
And one of the things that these trees live with and live through, and actually can benefit from, is fire.
They have this incredibly thick fireproof bark, I forget how thick, like a foot thick.
And the mature trees have their first limbs really high up in the air, like 100 feet up, halfway up.
So the needles and little branches aren't anywhere near where the fire is likely to be.
So they don't catch on fire very easily at all.
And they actually kind of like fire.
It clears away the underbrush between them.
And they have these small, sealed-up-tight cones.
The heat from the fires causes the cones to pop open and the seeds to fly out.
And then those seeds can germinate on this newly cleared land, right?
Kind of amazing.
In fact, I even read a little factoid, I didn't know this, that these tight little cones can hold green viable seeds for 20 years, waiting for the next fire to send them out.
Or some other things can also cause the seeds to get out, but fire is the main thing.
So these guys live in a whole different kind of time.
They're not trying to squeeze anything in.
They're fire adapted and fire dependent, both.
But, and you probably already guessed what the but is, they're not adapted for the megafires that we've been seeing these last few years.
These incredibly hot, fast fires that sweep through, and the firefighters each year say, "This is the worst we've ever seen in our whole lives."
The hotter climate, the denser brush, a century of fire suppression, there are a lot of factors, but the fires are much different, much hotter than they were for the previous thousands of years.
And so in 2020, there was one fire that swept through several sequoia groves and killed 9,000, at least 9,000, mature giant sequoias.
Fourteen percent of the entire population in one fire event.
In one year, right?
Put that against 2,000, 3,000.
It's 15,000 years since the last glaciation.
So I think when I first read that, I was reading it on my phone probably, right?
Reading the headlines.
I think I just put my phone away, and I couldn't really cope with that and put it out of my mind and got back to my squeezing-time business.
But this time, hearing the actual voices of the NPR hosts and the scientists, and of course they always have a sound bite of somebody out in the field, right?
Measuring the tree and looking up and saying, "Yes, there's no sign of life."
This massive, massive 2,000-year-old tree.
It just sunk in.
Made me cry a little bit.
Made me remember, I knew that we're living in a burning world, in a time of huge change.
And of course, that's always been so.
The Buddha used that exact metaphor 2,500 years ago.
"Monks, this world is burning," he said, in a really famous early sutta.
He didn't mean exactly forest fires, but still, this world is burning, changing, suffering.
We are suffering.

But from a scientific frame that he wouldn't have had so much, it's also true that in the history of the planet, as we can understand it from the evidence, there have always been massive changes, including, depending on which measure you're looking at, times when one thing or the other changes much more quickly for a while.
And one of those is extinctions.
There have been other periods of mass extinction over a relatively short period, like is happening now, and may well happen to a large extent to these wonderful trees.
Maybe in the end there'll just be a few specimens in botanical gardens and neighborhoods, and the native groves will be gone.
Could happen in our lifetime.
But there have been previous times that stuff like this has happened.
It's not the only time.
So how do we hold multiple perspectives like that?
How can that help us to cope and function and try to be actually helpful?

Of course, a famous example is 66 million years ago, which is a fairly small amount of time compared to the history of the planet, 4.7 or 6 billion years, only 66 million years ago when the dinosaurs vanished.
So now they're pretty sure about the theory of at least one huge meteor landing on the Yucatan peninsula in Mexico.
And then probably they figured out several other asteroids.
Meteor, I'm sure I forget the difference.
Asteroids, I guess, is the name, hit the planet and huge dust storms and an asteroid-induced nuclear winter happened, and the dinosaurs were gone in short order.

They can't tell if that was thousands of years or hundreds of thousands of years against the scale of millions, but in a relatively short time there was a huge change in what creatures live on our planet.
Huge change.
So it's happening now too.
There have been two or three other mass extinction events over our geologic history.
And yet your mind is probably saying, "Well, that's different.
It's bad luck, getting hit by an asteroid."
Yeah, maybe so.
But we also know from Buddhism and science both that everything happens according to cause and effect, right?
According to karma.
So the whole universe somehow lined up for a huge asteroid to hit the planet 66 million years ago.

And then the whole universe lined up a couple hundred thousand years ago for Homo sapiens to evolve and be really good with tools and really interested in changing things around and getting stuff done and getting more comfortable, or just changing things.
I don't know what exactly motivates us.
So in a way, of course we need to own this.
It's our species' responsibility.
And yet we are also functioning in the world of karma, which isn't exactly all progress, right?
I was talking to them last night about the myth of progress.
For one thing, I learned recently from a podcast about anthropology that most hunter-gatherer societies were working less than half time, I think it was like 14 to 16 hours or something like that.
So that's all the work you need to do to get all the food and shelter you need.
We work a lot harder, apparently, trying to squeeze in things.
But anyway, here we are in the midst of the climate catastrophe.
And it's really hard to accept that I myself, my own life and my choices and my actions, have contributed to the danger to these trees that I love.
I have driven a lot of miles in cars over my lifetime, hundreds of thousands of miles probably.
It's a lot of emissions.
And I live in a house, which is also part of the problem.
An old house, probably a little worse.
And I'm afraid you're probably part of the problem too.

I guess what I'm trying to say is that as we accept this stuff, and some of us are slow to the party, I'm sure, I know I feel like I am, as we accept this and take it in, it becomes more possible to do something.
We can all do different kinds of things.
It's also deeply embedded in our privilege and status.
I was lucky to have the resources to put a heat pump in my house.
I'm tempted to spend the whole Dharma talk on science, so I'll try to restrain myself, but heat pumps are amazing, actually.
You should look them up.
They don't work like other heaters.
They don't just use energy to generate heat.
A gas heater is probably 50, 60, 70 percent efficient, 90-something if you have a really new one and everything's really well done.
That means that of all the energy you put into it, gas energy or electric energy, you get somewhere between 50 and 90 percent back in heat, heating your house.
And then there's the question of how much leaks out because of your insulation, isn't that great, right?
Well, a heat pump can be up to 600 percent efficient.
Isn't that crazy?
So we are clever, humans.
We create the problem and then we think of amazing technologies that can also help.
Yeah, a heat pump can make six times more heat energy than the electricity you put into it.
It has to do with making use of phase changes, like a refrigerator.
You're basically running a giant refrigerator in reverse to heat your house.
But then it's easy for any of us, me, to say, "Oh good, I did that."
I was writing about my happiness of installing a heat pump and being able to afford it, pretty much just afford it.
And now I look across at the neighboring building, which I also own, and I remember that it has gas heaters and no insulation in the attic yet.
Oops, there's more to go, always more to go.
If you're interested in this particular part of climate change: buildings, it turns out, mostly heating them, produce about half of the climate change gases.
So it's not just cars and industry, it's us turning up the thermostat who are heating the planet.
But anyway, if you're interested in working on this in your home, there's a wonderful new program.
I just found out about this, actually through our Climate Justice Interfaith Group.
If you're in Bellingham, I think it's just Bellingham, it's called the Community Energy Challenge.
So look that up.
They'll come and do a low-cost assessment of your house, and they can even subsidize to some extent the work that they recommend to reduce your carbon footprint from living in your house.
I think everyone here is probably lucky enough to live in a house.
So these are hard realities to face and accept.
And it's not an all-or-nothing proposition.
So maybe today I accepted a little more that I'm helping to kill the giant sequoias, as horrible as that is.
And not just to get busy and geek out on the science and put some more of my savings into energy efficiency, but to actually feel that too.

Can I let myself feel the sorrow and the horror of this situation and the many contradictions and confusions in it, that we humans are part of this big system that's always changing, and that it's our fault in a way?
It's also a natural consequence of more factors than we can ever understand.
And here it is.
And here it is.
So of course our practice helps.
And lately I've been exploring a new Suzuki Roshi, Shunryu Suzuki Roshi, the Western founder of our lineage.
On my little lineage chart, I think he's my great-great-grandfather.
The chapter that I've gotten to now to speak about is his chapter on breathing, which we do all the time.
Our practice encourages us to meet breathing in a fresh way.
It really seems to radically support this possibility of acceptance and dropping in more deeply to things as they are.
So I want to share a little bit of that chapter and make a few comments.
And then I'll be curious to have a little time to discuss all this with you, whether you want to talk about heat pumps or meditation or something else entirely.
So here's the first couple of paragraphs of the breathing chapter of *Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind*.
*When we practice zazen, our mind always follows our breathing.
When we inhale, the air comes into the inner world.
When we exhale, the air goes out into the outer world.
The inner world is limitless and the outer world is limitless.
We say inner world or outer world, but actually there's just one whole world.*
*In this limitless world, our throat is like a swinging door.
The air comes in and goes out like someone passing through a swinging door.
If you think I breathe, the I is extra.
There's no you to say I.
What we call I is just a swinging door that moves when we inhale and when we exhale.
It just moves.
That is all.
When your mind is pure and calm enough to follow this movement, there is nothing, no I, no world, no mind, no body, just a swinging door.*
*When you practice zazen, all that exists is the movement of the breathing, but we are aware of this movement.
You should not be absent-minded, but to be aware of the movement does not mean to be aware with your small self, but rather to be aware of your universal nature, buddha nature.
This kind of awareness is very important because we're usually so one-sided.
Our usual understanding of life is dualistic, you and I, this and that, good and bad, but actually these discriminations are themselves the awareness of universal existence.
You means to be aware of the universe in the form of you.
I means to be aware of it in the form of I.
You and I are both just swinging doors.
This kind of understanding is necessary.
This should not even be called understanding.
It's actually the true experience of life through zazen practice.*
So what are we setting aside when we [unclear: "feel the feeling and really am and are"] the swinging door?
I was playing with this a little bit in zazen today, and it feels a little bit forced to feel the sliding door or the swinging door in my throat like he suggests.
What I notice is I feel the swinging door in the diaphragm.
Remember how it works: there's this diaphragm muscle stretched across the bottom of your rib cage, and it contracts, pulls down.
I'm in a science mood today.
So the pressure goes down in your lungs and air flows in, right, and then it relaxes and the pressure differential is gone and the air flows out again.
But I was really feeling more than I've ever felt before, I think, the feeling of this diaphragm muscle opening, closing, in, out.
It felt kind of like a jellyfish.
Have you ever watched a jellyfish swim?
So graceful.
I noticed too that I've always had this sort of orientation towards the exhalation.
There's a feeling right in the exhalation that I've always treasured and maybe want when I sit down.
So I gave more space to the evenness of this, because of course it's not one over the other, right?
There's only inhalation and exhalation, and the inhale is also a sense of opening, arriving, energy, right?
So we're arriving and letting go, arriving and letting go, energizing and releasing.
And this natural flow, there's nothing out of place, right?
There's nothing that shouldn't be there that is there, there's nothing that should be there that isn't there.
It's only this breathing, this embodiment, this moment, this whole limitless world, like he says, arising and passing away within us.
And then I don't know if I quite have language to bridge this exactly to what I was saying before, but somehow it does.
Somehow zazen expresses, holds, lands us, brings us, reminds us, is us as the amazing beings we are who can accept the catastrophe and show up in the middle of it with helping hands.
Not blind to it, not like also sad, worried, also encouraged, also excited, also engaged, right?
So maybe you could connect some of those things, the inhale and the exhale, I suppose, if you wanted to.
But somehow with our practice in our lives and this wonderful supportive practice we have through being in a practice community, I was appreciating that yesterday when we did our sit in the park.
We went to one of the Bellingham city parks that has this nice covered pavilion, in case it drizzled.
It didn't, but in case.
But also a sense of, on the one hand, containment: we're inside this pavilion.
On the other hand, totally open to the world.
It's just a railing and a roof, and the world flowed into us as wind and sound and other people in the park.
There were three young women practicing their volleyball moves who brought a boombox, kind of peaceful music, actually, too.

Kids playing, church bells ringing, and we spent two hours today doing, two hours yesterday, nothing but breathing in and breathing out, sitting, walking, sitting, walking, quietly together, but together.
So it's so easy for us to think of all this as an individual endeavor, which is odd since we're in the middle of this huge system that co-created the catastrophe and the beauty and the joy.
So Suzuki Roshi here is talking about I and me, a swinging door inside us, but he's also talking about we and us, swinging doors for each other, with each other.
As you inhale, I inhale.
As you exhale, I exhale.
And just like my individual experience of breathing, this is always true, right?
We're always connected in this way.

But this practice that we somehow were fortunate enough to receive and show up for and endure the quirkiness and the unpleasant aspects of, right, the uncomfortable moments, I don't know why people stick around, but we do.
Maybe on some deep level our heart, our bodies, our big minds know this is a path.
This is a path to something bigger than just me.
And I know I'll forget about it again and get lost in my story and my privilege and my confusion and my self-centeredness, but that swinging door is always swinging, right?
That amoeba is always swimming.
I'm always getting worried and then relaxing again, right?
Accepting again so that I can show up.
A little later in the chapter, at the end of this little chapter, I'll skip to that, after quite a little meditation on time, so we could do a few much more explorations of time.
Suzuki wrote in this chapter, kind of gives his own version of Dogen's Being-Time essay, because how does all this relate to being in time?
Of course we can't avoid that.
We are beings in time, and time and beings.
But then he concludes with this.
*When we become truly ourselves, we just become a swinging door.
And we are purely independent of and at the same time dependent upon everything.
Without air we cannot breathe.
Each of one of us is the midst of myriads of worlds.
We're in the center of the world always, the center of our world, always, moment after moment.
So we are completely dependent and completely independent.
If you have this kind of experience, this kind of existence, you will have absolute independence.
You will not be bothered by anything.
So when you practice zazen and your mind should be concentrated on your breathing, this kind of activity is the fundamental activity of the universal being.
Without this experience, this practice, it's impossible to attain absolute freedom.*
He could pack a lot in.
That's Suzuki Roshi.
And these are mostly off-the-cuff talks, it's amazing.
Let's just highlight a thing or two before I close the formal talk.

The key thing he's saying is that we understand, and this is not a head thing, maybe the mind is of course always involved, it's a felt experience, that we're independent of everything and totally dependent on everything, right?
We're one, we're two.
Sometimes they summarize that by saying we're not two, which isn't one and isn't two, right?
We're in the middle of it and we're each our own experience and manifestation of it.
We're in the center of our world, and it's not our world.
It's everyone's world that we're in the center of.
And I don't know about this practice exactly.
The way he talked about this practice, Soto Zen as he's describing it, he says without that it's impossible to be free.
I don't know about that so much, but maybe without some kind of practice it's impossible to be free.
Otherwise it's just that our conditioning gets wound up.
We get born like one of those little wind-up [unclear: "tiles"], top toys.
The key gets wound up really tight and we go around for some years.
We don't know how long, and then we fall over.
But this practice allows a different approach.
We feel that pressure, right?
We feel that key.
We feel that desire to squeeze something in.
We feel that fear.
We feel that sense of impotence and inadequacy and all that.
But we also can feel the swinging door and know that we're completely independent, dependent, completely flowing, completely free at the same time.
And we aren't bound by our idea of our boundness anymore.
Okay, that's probably enough on that.
Thanks for listening to all that.
I'll chant us out and stop, and then we can stop the recording and see what thoughts or feelings we want to exchange.
*Our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*

verbatim.text: Got it, Zoom Lady. Okay. There's a little opening chant. Please chant along if you know it or whatever you want to do. An unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas. Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the tathagata's words. Good morning again, everybody.
